snapshots.name: Socrates
snapshots.subtitle: Predecessor Aristotle argues against
snapshots.body: The philosopher Aristotle repeatedly invokes and revises. Socrates had argued that virtue is a form of knowledge and that no one does wrong knowingly; Aristotle credits the insight but insists Socrates was wrong to make virtue purely intellectual, since it also requires habituated character.

snapshots.name: Plato
snapshots.subtitle: Aristotle's teacher
snapshots.body: Aristotle's teacher and the source of the theory of a single, separate Form of the Good, which Aristotle politely but firmly rejects in Book I as unhelpful for a practical inquiry into how a person should actually live. Plato is also credited with the method of arguing both from and toward first principles.

snapshots.name: Solon
snapshots.subtitle: Athenian statesman
snapshots.body: The Athenian lawgiver credited with the maxim that no one should be called happy until his life has ended. Aristotle uses the saying to test whether happiness can depend on how a whole life, including its final fortunes, turns out.

snapshots.name: Priam
snapshots.subtitle: King of Troy in Homer
snapshots.body: The Trojan king whose old age, in Homer's telling, collapsed from prosperity into ruin. Aristotle uses his reversal of fortune as the hard case for whether a happy life can be undone by later disaster.

snapshots.name: The Good for Man (Eudaimonia)
snapshots.subtitle: The book's governing question
snapshots.body: What Aristotle calls the chief good, the end at which all human action ultimately aims: not a fleeting feeling but an activity of the soul in accordance with virtue over a complete life, commonly rendered "happiness" or "flourishing." Every book of the Ethics circles back to defining and defending it.

snapshots.name: The Doctrine of the Mean
snapshots.subtitle: How virtue is located
snapshots.body: The claim, developed in Book II, that moral virtue is a settled disposition to feel and act at the intermediate point between an excess and a deficiency — courage, for instance, standing between rashness and cowardice. The mean is relative to the person and situation, not a fixed arithmetical midpoint.

snapshots.name: Habituation
snapshots.subtitle: How virtue is acquired
snapshots.body: Aristotle's answer to how moral virtue is formed: not by nature and not by instruction alone, but by repeatedly doing virtuous acts until they become settled habits of character, the way a person becomes a builder by building. Lawgivers rely on exactly this mechanism to make citizens good.

snapshots.name: Practical Wisdom (Phronesis)
snapshots.subtitle: The intellectual virtue of action
snapshots.body: The capacity, discussed in Book VI, to deliberate well about what is good for oneself and for people generally, and to see correctly what a particular situation calls for. Aristotle distinguishes it sharply from mere cleverness and from the theoretical virtues of art and science.

snapshots.name: Imperfect Self-Control
snapshots.subtitle: Acting against one's own better judgment
snapshots.body: The condition, examined in Book VII, of a person who knows what is right yet is overcome by appetite and acts against that knowledge anyway — as opposed to the vicious person, who acts wrongly because his judgment itself is corrupted. Aristotle treats it as a puzzle Socrates' theory of virtue-as-knowledge cannot explain.

snapshots.name: Friendship (Philia)
snapshots.subtitle: Two books devoted to it
snapshots.body: The subject of Books VIII and IX, treated as necessary for a complete life and as the bond that holds communities together. Aristotle distinguishes friendships of utility and pleasure, which are fragile, from friendship grounded in virtue between good people, which alone is durable and complete.
